title: Ear Canal Foreign Body / Cerumen Removal Under Microscope
linked_topic: Ear and Nasal Foreign Body Removal
source_label: Pasha 6e and Cummings 7e (Infections of the External Ear; Topical Therapies of External Ear Disorders)
indications: Symptomatic or obstructing cerumen impaction (hearing loss, fullness, pain, need to see the TM) and any canal foreign body. Button batteries are an emergency requiring same-day removal because current-driven and alkaline injury can perforate the TM and damage the canal, ossicles and facial nerve within hours; do not irrigate them. Live insects should be immobilized with mineral oil or lidocaine before removal. Vegetable matter swells with water, so irrigation is avoided. Irrigation is also contraindicated with known or suspected perforation, prior ear surgery, tubes, or the only hearing ear. Uncooperative children, deeply impacted objects near the TM, failed prior attempts, or canal trauma warrant removal under general anesthesia.
setup: Binocular microscope with assorted speculums; good restraint or assistant for children, or brief general anesthesia by mask
Instruments: right-angle hooks, alligator and cup forceps, ring curettes, Frazier and Schuknecht suctions in several sizes
Mineral oil or 2% lidocaine for insects; cerumenolytics for hard wax (water- or oil-based)
Irrigation setup only when the TM is known intact and object is not organic or a battery
Tissue glue (cyanoacrylate on a stick) only for smooth spherical objects in cooperative patients, used cautiously
landmarks: Cartilaginous lateral canal (hair, cerumen glands; less painful)
Bony-cartilaginous junction and isthmus (narrowest, objects lodge medial to it)
Bony medial canal with thin, sensitive skin
Anterior canal recess and tympanic annulus
Tympanic membrane and handle of malleus
danger: Pushing the object medially past the isthmus or into the middle ear
Canal laceration and bleeding obscuring the field
Button battery injury progressing in hours
steps: History and object type

Identify what the object is (battery, organic, smooth bead, sharp, insect), duration, prior attempts, and history of perforation, tubes or ear surgery. Examine the opposite ear and nostrils in children, who often have multiple foreign bodies.
Prepare the patient

Position supine for children with a parent or assistant stabilizing the head, or use general anesthesia when cooperation is poor or the object is medial. For adults, a seated or reclined position works. Explain each step and warn about pressure and noise.
Visualize first

Use the largest speculum that fits comfortably, straightening the canal by pulling the pinna up and back in adults or back and down in infants. Under the microscope, define the edges of the object and the space around it before touching anything.
Kill and immobilize insects

Instill mineral oil or lidocaine to kill a live insect, which eases pain and stops movement. Then remove it with forceps or suction. Lidocaine can cause brief vertigo if it reaches the middle ear through an unrecognized perforation.
Grasp irregular objects

Use alligator or cup forceps for soft or irregular objects with an edge, such as paper or foam. Avoid forceps on smooth, round objects because they slip and push medially. Remove in one controlled movement while watching through the microscope.
Hook behind round objects

For beads and balls, slide a right-angle hook or ring curette past the object along a gap, rotate it behind, and roll the object laterally. Suction with a soft tip can also capture smooth objects that occupy most of the lumen.
Remove button batteries promptly

Remove batteries the same day with forceps or suction, then inspect for burns, perforation and canal necrosis. Do not irrigate or use drops before removal. Document injury carefully, and arrange close follow-up for stenosis, perforation or facial nerve involvement.
Cerumen removal

Remove soft wax with suction and hard plugs with curettes, working lateral to medial along the canal floor, not against the thin superior or anterior bony skin. Soften very hard plugs with drops for several days or irrigate with body-temperature water when the TM is intact.
Inspect after removal

Examine the entire canal and the TM for retained fragments, lacerations or perforation, and check hearing grossly. Lacerations heal well on their own; a perforation warrants an audiogram and follow-up to confirm healing.
Escalate when needed

Stop after one or two failed attempts in an awake child to avoid trauma and loss of cooperation. Proceed to removal under general anesthesia, or rarely a postauricular approach for deeply impacted objects or those in the middle ear.
exit_check: Object completely removed with no fragments or second object remaining
TM integrity documented and canal injuries noted
Gross hearing and facial nerve function intact
postop: Dry-ear precautions if a laceration or perforation is present
Topical drops only to treat established otitis externa, not routinely
Audiogram and follow-up for perforation, battery injuries, or hearing concerns
Counsel on avoiding cotton swabs and safe storage of batteries

early: Vertigo from cold irrigation or caloric effect
late: Canal stenosis after battery or chemical injury
Conductive hearing loss from ossicular injury

attending_followup: Why is a button battery in the ear an emergency?

Current flow generates hydroxide at the negative pole, causing liquefactive necrosis within hours. It can perforate the TM, destroy canal skin and ossicles, and rarely injure the facial nerve. Remove immediately; never irrigate.
Known or suspected TM perforation, tympanostomy tubes, prior ear surgery, vegetable or organic foreign bodies that swell, button batteries, and an only hearing ear.
Where do objects lodge and why does it matter?
Medial to the isthmus at the bony-cartilaginous junction. Medial canal skin is thin and sensitive, so manipulation there is painful and bleeds easily; push-past risk to the TM is greatest.
Coughing on stimulation of the posterior canal skin, mediated by the auricular branch of the vagus nerve.
Kill it first with mineral oil or lidocaine, then remove with forceps or suction under the microscope.
